## An unanticipated threshold, enforced by financiers

:::::: columns
::: column
- Operating wind facility in an emerging-market jurisdiction: national wildlife legislation does not yet set species-specific mortality limits for bats
- Project financing requires compliance with lender performance standards that mirror EU biodiversity norms in substance, if not in legal force
- Fixed annual bat-fatality thresholds were imposed per site by that process, with no documented derivation available
- Year 1 of operation: observed mortality exceeded what was operationally acceptable -- an emergency operational response was required, not anticipated at design stage
:::

::: column
**Two standards, one project**

No binding national species-mortality limit

&#8595;

Lender-imposed, EU-aligned threshold applied anyway
:::
::::::

## Potential Biological Removal as the operational anchor

:::::: columns
::: column
- With no documented derivation for the imposed thresholds, and no independent local-abundance estimate for the species, the analysis works backwards from the numbers already in force
- Frick et al. (2026) adapt the classical, marine-mammal-derived PBR concept to bat mortality at wind facilities -- addressing low fecundity, delayed maturity and high sensitivity to adult survival
- PBR becomes the shared language for reverse-engineering what assumptions the imposed thresholds are implicitly consistent with
:::

::: column
**PBR = ½ · Rmax · Fr · Nmin**

- Rmax = λmax − 1 -- maximum population growth rate
- Fr -- recovery factor, linked to IUCN status
- Nmin -- conservative lower-bound local abundance

λmax standardised via the Niel & Lebreton (2005) demographic-invariant approximation from adult survival (s) and age at first breeding (α).
:::
::::::

## λmax from demography: the Niel & Lebreton (2005) approximation

:::::: columns
::: column
- Niel & Lebreton (2005): a closed-form λmax approximation from just two demographic parameters -- adult survival (s) and age at first breeding (α) -- avoiding a full, poorly-constrained vital-rate schedule
- Frick et al. (2026) use it to set PRECAUTIONARY, FIXED λmax values -- 1.24 (most bats), 1.20 (later-maturing families, e.g. Pteropodidae) -- not a fitted, species-specific growth rate
- A documented, counterintuitive relationship: λmax *decreases* as adult survival or age at first breeding increase -- a life-history trade-off built into the approximation itself, not a sign of decline
:::

::: column
**λmax(s, α) -- Niel & Lebreton (2005)**

λmax ≈ [(sα − s + α + 1) + √D] / (2α)

where D = (s − sα − α − 1)² − 4sα²

- s -- adult survival (annual probability)
- α -- age at first breeding (years)

*The same two inputs behind every λmax value used in this note, fixed or realistic. λmax stays above 1 (a growing population) throughout the realistic range explored.*
:::
::::::

## A Poisson-based weekly control chart, not an annual pass/fail line

:::::: columns
::: column
- Mortality risk concentrates in migration windows -- a flat, linear share of the annual reference misreads how much of the season's risk has already passed
- The annual reference is converted into an expected cumulative trajectory (same seasonal shape as mortality itself), with Poisson-based statistical control limits around it
- Each tier maps to an escalation step on the turbines already identified as critical: maintain (GREEN) / intensify, e.g. a lower cut-in (AMBER) / escalate to a wider subset and the most conservative cut-in, and trigger a structured review (RED)
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_control_chart`)
:::
::::::

## 2026 mortality position: two different questions, two different answers

:::::: columns
::: column
Reading year-to-date and year-over-year together is what resolves what would otherwise look like two inconsistent percentages for the same intervention.

- Both projects' 2026 corrected estimate already exceeds the annual reference for the year to date -- driven overwhelmingly by the weeks *before* curtailment began on 5 May, not by the response itself
- Read year-over-year instead, through the same week: Project 1 is 59% lower than the equivalent 2025 period; Project 2 only 5% lower -- a real reduction at both, but markedly smaller at the second, worth watching
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_ytd_vs_yoy`)
:::
::::::

## Does a simple turbine ranking recover the real selection?

:::::: columns
::: column
The turbines actually curtailed were selected under a separate, lender-agreed GenEst procedure -- not this note's own methodology. Two checks against that real selection, on the same slide.

- An independent ranking (raw carcasses + this note's own working factor) recovers most of the real selection, and a larger share of its mortality than of its turbine count
- That same check is what drove replacing a single flat/combined GenEst factor with two project-specific ones: Project 2's true aggregate ratio (6.2x) sits well above what a shared 4x or 4.3x median would have assumed, understating its corrected mortality by roughly a third
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_turbine_validation`)
:::
::::::

## Observed mortality fell well below the no-curtailment counterfactual

:::::: columns
::: column
![](`r params$fig_reduction_results`)
:::

::: column
**Reading the result**

- This asks a different, more targeted question: only the operational weeks the response has actually been running, not the full year (which includes months of pre-curtailment mortality)
- Turbines were deliberately curtailed because of high historical mortality, not assigned at random, and only one untreated reference year exists
- This is operational effectiveness evidence, not a randomised causal estimate of curtailment efficacy -- and a checkpoint (21 weeks of real 2026 data so far), not a final verdict
:::
::::::

# What is PBR actually bounding?

## A fixed λmax removes one uncertainty, not all of them

:::::: columns
::: column
*Frick et al. (2026) is fast becoming the reference methodology for bat-mortality thresholds at wind facilities worldwide. It retains PBR's precautionary structure -- but several of its uncertainties are not resolved by a fixed λmax alone.*

- λmax fixed at 1.24 (most bats) / 1.20 (later-maturing families) -- a precautionary ceiling, not a fitted, species-specific growth rate
- But λmax is far more sensitive to adult survival than to age at first breeding -- and adult survival is among the least well-constrained parameters for most bat species
- A fixed λmax controls one source of sensitivity; it does not remove the underlying uncertainty in how that ceiling was set
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_lambda_elasticity`)
:::
::::::

## The thresholds are not pinned down by a single assumption

:::::: columns
::: column
- Backsolving the local abundance (Nmin) consistent with each imposed threshold, under Frick's own two fixed λmax benchmarks, gives a wide implied range -- not a single number
- No shared population size reproduces both sites' thresholds under either benchmark
- A plausible range is the honest answer here -- not a false precision inherited from reporting only one point estimate
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_nmin_range`)
:::
::::::

# Why anchor removal to a pessimistic Nmin, rather than to carrying capacity?

## Sustainable removal near carrying capacity

:::::: columns
::: column
*An alternative reference point: classic logistic (Schaefer) surplus-production logic.*

A constant harvest H has a stable equilibrium at the population level N = α·K.

**H(α) = r · K · α · (1 − α)**

Staying close to K (an ecological-viability standard) implies a much smaller sustainable H than classic MSY at α = 0.5.
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_schaefer_curve`)
:::
::::::

## How far can plausible biology push the comparison? {.exploratory}

:::::: columns
::: column
- Holding the most favourable adult-survival estimate found across this species and its closest relatives -- not the realistic rate -- the sustainable removal under a carrying-capacity standard rises markedly
- It still falls short of either current imposed threshold, and nowhere near requires Frick's λmax benchmarks to hold
- The comparison remains sensitive to which standard is adopted: distance-from-extinction (PBR) or distance-from-K (carrying capacity)

*Exploratory -- not part of the reviewed technical note.*
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_cc_vs_pbr`)
:::
::::::

## FCS speaks the language of carrying capacity, not extinction

:::::: columns
::: column
**Habitats Directive, Art. 1(i)**

"Favourable" conservation status requires a population "maintaining itself ... as a viable component of its natural habitats", with "sufficiently large habitat to maintain its populations on a long-term basis."

**Epstein, López-Bao & Chapron (2015)**

Commission guidance frames FCS as "distance from a favourable state", not distance from extinction -- "it is more logically consistent to measure FCS from carrying capacity than from extinction."
:::

::: column
![](`r params$fig_fcs_spectrum`)

Current operational practice sits near the extinction end; the European legal frame points toward the opposite one.
:::
::::::

## Open questions for the workshop

1. Should an operational mortality threshold be required to state a plausible range, not a single point value?
2. Where should the biological-envelope evidence come from when species-specific data are this thin -- congeneric or confamilial literature?
3. Is an Nmin / distance-from-extinction standard (PBR), or a carrying-capacity / FCS-aligned standard, the right reference for projects held to EU-equivalent lender standards outside the EU?
4. What would it take for an operational threshold to be defensible as FCS-aligned -- not merely precautionary?
